html:
In 109 and 108 BCE the armies of Emperor Wu of Han invaded Gojoseon, the oldest Korean state, and took its capital Wanggeom near today's Pyongyang, in North Korea.

Gojoseon had grown strong in the north of the peninsula and southern Manchuria and blocked trade with the south. After a year of hard war its court split, a minister killed the king, and the city fell. The Han set up four commanderies on its land.

The most lasting was Lelang, centred near Pyongyang, which lasted until Goguryeo took it in 313. Through Lelang, Chinese writing, iron, lacquer and ideas of government flowed into Korea and on to Japan. North Korea today stresses Gojoseon as the root of the nation, and in the 1990s it built a great tomb for Dangun, its legendary founder.
